title: Red teaming, penetration testing and purple teaming
concept: Red teaming evaluates an objective across people, process and technology. A penetration test often concentrates on vulnerabilities in a defined scope; purple teaming coordinates testing with defenders.
deeper: These approaches overlap. Define the decision the exercise should inform before selecting techniques or tools.
practice: Compare a web-app test, a simulated account-compromise exercise and a joint detection validation. Write a measurable objective for each.
question: Is the number of compromised hosts a sufficient success metric?
answer: No. Measure the agreed business objective and defensive outcomes, including evidence and limitations.

title: Rules of engagement and authorization
concept: Record permitted assets, identities, techniques, times, data handling, contacts and stop conditions before execution.
deeper: Third-party services and shared infrastructure need separate scope decisions. A domain name can resolve to infrastructure the organization does not own.
practice: Fill out the workbook engagement template for a localhost exercise. Include a stop contact and explicit excluded actions.
question: Does discovering a new asset automatically add it to scope?
answer: No. Validate ownership and obtain an updated scope decision.

title: Repeatable lab design
concept: Use disposable systems, synthetic identities and controlled networking. A baseline snapshot supports repeatable experiments.
deeper: Shared folders, cloud credentials and host integrations can cross lab boundaries. A snapshot does not undo external side effects.
practice: Draw a lab with an operator, one test service and a logging source. Identify every connection leaving that boundary.
question: What needs recording before a test?
answer: Build versions, starting state, credentials used, expected effects, evidence collection and rollback.

title: Threat-informed objectives
concept: Choose relevant adversary behaviors based on assets, exposure and business impact rather than copying an entire campaign.
deeper: A realistic scenario can test a single boundary deeply. Historical adversary reports may omit details or reflect environments unlike yours.
practice: Model a fictional notes service and define the consequence of a test user accessing another test user record.
question: Does naming an adversary make an exercise realistic?
answer: No. Relevance depends on behavior, prerequisites and environment.

title: ATT&CK and emulation planning
concept: Map the behavior being exercised to ATT&CK and identify telemetry needed to observe it. Use emulation plans as references, not automatic execution scripts.
deeper: Technique labels describe behaviors, not permission to perform them or proof of detection coverage.
practice: Build a three-column plan: behavior, required starting condition and expected defender evidence.
question: Does a successful test prove the SOC can respond?
answer: No. Collection, alerting, triage and response must each be verified.

title: Reconnaissance and asset validation
concept: Start with supplied inventories and authorized passive sources. Distinguish a lead from a verified in-scope asset.
deeper: Certificates, DNS records and public code can be stale or shared. Minimize collection of personal or irrelevant information.
practice: Compare a fictional inventory with three supplied hostnames and classify verified, uncertain and excluded assets.
question: Can a search-engine result establish ownership?
answer: No. Confirm ownership and scope through the engagement process.

title: Bounded service discovery
concept: Discovery identifies reachable services from a specific test location. Bound ports, targets and rates to answer a concrete question.
deeper: Open ports do not prove vulnerabilities; closed or filtered results depend on the path and sensor location.
practice: Run the loopback Nmap exercise in the workbook and compare it with curl and server logs.
question: Does one source location prove network-wide reachability?
answer: No. Routing, filtering and identity can change access from other locations.

title: Web and API assessment workflow
concept: Trace inputs, authentication, authorization and data flow in an owned training application. Use two synthetic users to test ownership boundaries.
deeper: A client-side restriction does not establish server enforcement. Separate session handling from object-level and function-level authorization.
practice: Use Burp Proxy history to inspect a harmless request to the local fixture. For an owned staging app, document expected denial before testing a cross-account request.
question: Does a successful HTTP response establish access to protected data?
answer: No. Inspect response content and the server-side decision.

title: Identity and access-path modeling
concept: Accounts, roles, groups and delegated rights form paths to sensitive actions. Model who can act as whom and under which prerequisites.
deeper: An apparent graph path may be blocked by configuration, policy or missing privileges. Treat it as a hypothesis until validated.
practice: Draw a fictional access graph with a test user, support role and service identity. Identify a least-privilege correction.
question: Does a graph edge prove a complete compromise chain?
answer: No. Validate each prerequisite and transition in the approved lab.

title: Initial access and assumed-breach exercises
concept: An assumed-breach exercise starts from an explicitly granted test identity or lab host to isolate downstream defensive questions.
deeper: Document the artificial starting condition. Results from it do not prove an attacker could achieve initial access independently.
practice: Create a tabletop comparing a test account with a standard-user lab session and list what each can legitimately do.
question: Why state the assumed starting access?
answer: It prevents overstating the demonstrated attack path and helps interpret control coverage.

title: Privilege boundaries and misconfiguration
concept: Privilege escalation concerns crossing an authorization boundary, often involving excessive rights or unsafe configuration.
deeper: Finding a writable location or administrator role is not enough; explain the privileged action it could influence and its prerequisites.
practice: Review a supplied fictional service configuration and propose a least-privilege repair without modifying a production host.
question: What distinguishes a misconfiguration from a demonstrated impact?
answer: Evidence that the relevant principal can reach the sensitive operation under the stated conditions.

title: Segmentation and lateral-access validation
concept: Evaluate whether a test identity and source segment can reach only the services required by policy.
deeper: Reachability, authentication and authorization are separate gates. Shared management infrastructure can alter the intended boundary.
practice: Create an expected allow/deny matrix for two synthetic roles and three lab services. Record approved access checks and compare observed results.
question: Does a reachable port imply successful lateral movement?
answer: No. It establishes only one part of the path.

title: Atomic Red Team and Caldera concepts
concept: Atomic Red Team organizes small behavior tests; Caldera supports orchestrated adversary emulation. Both require review of actual actions and effects.
deeper: Tests and prerequisites may download files, change settings or leave artifacts. Automation can amplify a poorly scoped action.
practice: Read one lab-relevant test definition without executing it. Inventory inputs, privileges, external dependencies, expected telemetry and cleanup steps.
question: Is a tool cleanup command proof of full restoration?
answer: No. Verify the baseline independently and account for external side effects.

title: Exercise infrastructure and communication controls
concept: An exercise may need a management channel, evidence storage and controlled test endpoints. Define ownership and retention for each.
deeper: A management channel introduces its own credentials and attack surface. Keep operator infrastructure access limited and auditable.
practice: Design a local-only control diagram and document how all connections and credentials will be removed at exercise end.
question: Does a familiar tool make its infrastructure secure automatically?
answer: No. Configuration, patching, access control and monitoring still matter.

title: Data-access and egress simulation
concept: Use synthetic canary records to demonstrate access or transfer objectives while minimizing collection. Agree on what constitutes sufficient proof.
deeper: Reading a record, staging it and transferring it cross different boundaries. A marker exercise has narrower realism than handling real sensitive data.
practice: Use a harmless marker file in the local HTTP fixture and correlate its retrieval with the server log. State that this is loopback transfer, not production egress testing.
question: Should demonstrating access require copying a whole dataset?
answer: No. Use the smallest approved evidence that supports the finding.

title: Human and physical assessment planning
concept: Human and physical tests evaluate processes such as reporting, identity verification and visitor handling when separately authorized.
deeper: Avoid collecting real passwords or unrelated personal information. Define participant protections, escalation and business-impact limits.
practice: Run a tabletop of a fictional suspicious-message report. Measure routing and verification decisions without sending deceptive messages.
question: Does a technical engagement automatically include phishing or physical entry?
answer: No. These need explicit scope and coordination.

title: Operator logs and reproducible evidence
concept: Record test identity, action, time, target, result and cleanup. Preserve raw observations separately from interpretation.
deeper: Clock differences and tool transformations can distort timelines. Hashes support integrity but not the truth of an observation.
practice: Create an operator record for the localhost scan and request. Correlate it with defender logs and note timezone conventions.
question: What makes a screenshot insufficient by itself?
answer: It may omit prerequisites, source data, timing or reproducible steps.

title: Purple-team validation and detection gaps
concept: Compare the operator action with sensor collection, parsing, analytic output, case handling and response. Locate the first failed stage.
deeper: An unalerted test may reflect missing telemetry or a rule gap; it is not automatically a stealth success. Likewise a test alert may not represent broad coverage.
practice: Use the SOC workbook to pair an action timeline with expected evidence and propose one measurable improvement.
question: What should a coverage claim include?
answer: The tested behavior, data source, rule version, environment, outcome and known limits.

title: Reporting, cleanup and retesting
concept: Report the objective, path, evidence, business consequence and prioritized repairs. Reconcile all introduced artifacts and test access.
deeper: Differentiate confirmed, conditional and untested paths. Retest after a fix and verify valid operations still work.
practice: Write an executive paragraph and a technical finding for the local exercise. Document normal behavior rather than inventing a vulnerability.
question: When is cleanup complete?
answer: When artifacts, credentials and settings have been reconciled against the agreed baseline and owners accept remaining items.

title: Red-team capstone and maturity planning
concept: Combine objective selection, rules of engagement, a bounded exercise, evidence and defender validation into a repeatable assessment.
deeper: Increase realism gradually according to learning goals, environment readiness and operational risk. A training exercise is not a claim of production compromise.
practice: Complete the supplied plan, perform the local observation exercise, correlate logs, record limitations and propose a follow-up purple-team test.
question: What demonstrates a useful outcome?
answer: A supported conclusion, clear defensive improvement, verified cleanup and an actionable retest plan.
